source.version: Journal version of record: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 8 (2026) 100302; received 15 February 2026, revised 25 March 2026, accepted 25 March 2026, available online 30 March 2026 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Who performs better? Exploring the role of generative AI in creativity and brainstorming

supplement.where: No supplement or online appendix is mentioned. The in-paper Appendix (p. 9: Fig. 1, Table 1, Table 2) is in this PDF. Data and preregistration at https://osf.io/h6ztr/ (p. 9, Data availability).
supplement.holds: Nothing beyond the PDF is referenced. Per-cell means and SDs for quantity and flexibility are not printed (only marginal means by factor in Table 1); they may be recoverable from the OSF data.

paper_design_summary: In a 2 x 2 between-subjects lab experiment, 212 undergraduates at a Midwestern US university brainstormed ideas for 10 minutes to improve a student orientation program, either alone or with Microsoft Copilot, while anticipating a later collaboration with either a human or an AI teammate. Trained undergraduate coders blind to condition scored each participant's ideas for quantity, originality, feasibility, fun, and flexibility (number of distinct categories), analyzed with 2 x 2 ANOVAs.

studies.label: Lab experiment: AI-assisted vs independent brainstorming x anticipated human vs AI teammate (SOAR orientation task)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Ideation condition (independent vs AI-assisted with Microsoft Copilot) crossed with anticipated teammate (human vs AI). The paper says participants were randomly assigned to the four conditions, but it also says the anticipated-teammate factor followed arrival: pairs who arrived together anticipated a human teammate and participants who arrived alone anticipated an AI teammate.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions (Independent/Anticipated human teammate = 69; AI-assisted/Anticipated human teammate = 68; Independent/Anticipated AI teammate = 37; AI-assisted/Anticipated AI teammate = 38).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 4 (Method); teammate assignment by arrival on p. 5, Section 4.2: "Participants who arrived alone were assigned to the condition anticipating an AI teammate."
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 3, Hypothesis 1 ("we pre-registered this hypothesis"); p. 4, Hypothesis 2; p. 9, Data availability: "This study was pre-registered at Open Science Framework", https://osf.io/h6ztr/. Hypotheses 3a and 3b (interactions) are stated as non-preregistered (pp. 3-4).

arms.name: Independent / Anticipated human teammate (HHT)
arms.description: Brainstormed alone; told the subsequent group session would be with a human partner (another participant present in the session).

arms.name: AI-assisted / Anticipated human teammate (AI-HHT)
arms.description: Brainstormed with Microsoft Copilot as an assisting tool; anticipated a human partner.

arms.name: Independent / Anticipated AI teammate (HAT)
arms.description: Brainstormed alone; anticipated an AI teammate (participants who arrived alone).

arms.name: AI-assisted / Anticipated AI teammate (AI-HAT)
arms.description: Brainstormed with Microsoft Copilot; anticipated an AI teammate (participants who arrived alone).

participants.exclusions: 224 participants were recruited. 10 failed condition-check items (did not correctly identify their anticipated partner or whether they received AI assistance) and were excluded; 2 more were excluded (one facilitator error in failing to provide the written handout, one language barrier). Final sample 212. The cell counts (69, 68, 37, 38) sum to 212 and are therefore post-exclusion. The paper does not give counts at assignment by condition.
participants.who: Undergraduate students (75.5% female; mean age 20.02, SD 1.67) at a large public Midwestern US university (UW-Madison per the IRB statement), participating for one extra course credit, with a $20 gift card for the top 25% of task performance.
participants.quote: A total of 224 participants were recruited for this in-person lab experiment at a large public university in the Midwestern United States. Ten participants failed the condition-check items

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Copilot (Auto mode), university-licensed; underlying model not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Each participant logged into an individual university Copilot account and was told to use it as an assisting tool, asking "what" and "how" questions or getting suggestions. Participants had to type out their own ideas and could not use AI-generated responses verbatim (pp. 4-5, Sections 4.2-4.3).

task.description: Individual brainstorming of ideas to improve or redesign the university's Student Orientation, Advising, and Registration (SOAR) program to make it more engaging and helpful; ideas typed into a Word document. This is the individual stage of a hybrid brainstorming procedure; the anticipated group session is a manipulation and its output is not analyzed.
task.duration: 10 minutes (extended from 8 minutes after a pilot) (p. 5, Section 4.3)

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Trained undergraduate coders blind to condition rated each idea on originality (novelty and uniqueness) on a 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) scale; participant score = mean across all of the participant's ideas. ICC .76 (first coding period, about 16% of ideas jointly coded by four coders) and .84 (second period, about 20% double-coded) (p. 5, Section 4.4).

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition: F(1, 208) = 16.78, eta^2 = .075, p < .001. Table 1: Independent M = 2.99, SD = .47; AI-Assisted M = 3.34, SD = .56. Marginal arm ns are not printed; cell ns on p. 4 (independent 69 + 37, AI-assisted 68 + 38). Interaction F(1, 208) = 7.61, eta^2 = .035, p = .006.
AI-assisted M = 3.49, SD = .59 vs independent M = 2.99, SD = .47, F(1, 135) = 29.94, eta^2 = .182; p < .001, 95% CI [.32, .68] (Bonferroni-adjusted simple effect). Cell ns 68 and 69 (p. 4).
AI-assisted M = 3.09, SD = .43 vs independent M = 2.99, SD = .48, F(1, 73) = .87, eta^2 = .012; p = .36. Cell ns 38 and 37 (p. 4).

outcomes.name: Fun (enjoyability) of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rated quality dimension: perceived enjoyability of each idea, 1 to 5 scale, same blind undergraduate coders; participant mean across ideas. ICC .71 (first period) and .75 (second period). The paper treats fun as a third component of idea quality, chosen because the task asks to make orientation more fun (pp. 2, 5).

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition: F(1, 208) = 4.23, eta^2 = .020, p = .041. Table 1: Independent M = 3.18, SD = .56; AI-Assisted M = 3.44, SD = .73. Interaction F(1, 208) = 9.58, eta^2 = .044, p = .002.
AI-assisted M = 3.01, SD = .59 vs independent M = 3.10, SD = .52, F(1, 73) = .50, eta^2 = .007; p = .48. Cell ns 38 and 37 (p. 4).

outcomes.name: Feasibility of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rated quality dimension: ease of implementation of each idea, 1 to 5 scale, same blind undergraduate coders; participant mean across ideas. ICC .70 (first period) and .78 (second period) (p. 5, Section 4.4).

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition: F(1, 208) = 2.71, eta^2 = .013, p = .101. Table 1: Independent M = 3.43, SD = .56; AI-Assisted M = 3.37, SD = .70. Interaction F(1, 208) = 10.80, eta^2 = .049, p = .001.
AI-assisted M = 3.51, SD = .66 vs independent M = 3.37, SD = .59, F(1, 135) = 1.85, eta^2 = .014; p = .176. Cell ns 68 and 69 (p. 4).

outcomes.name: Quantity of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total number of unique ideas typed by the participant in the Word document (p. 5, Section 4.4).

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition: F(1, 208) = 4.14, eta^2 = .020, p = .043. Table 1: Independent M = 13.24, SD = 5.8; AI-Assisted M = 11.69, SD = 7.00. Interaction F(1, 208) = 1.53, eta^2 = .007, p = .217 (no simple effects reported).

outcomes.name: Flexibility of ideas (number of distinct categories per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Trained coders blind to condition assigned each idea to one of thirteen mutually exclusive categories; flexibility = number of unique categories in the participant's idea list. Coders jointly coded 15 participants to establish consistency; no reliability coefficient is reported (p. 5, Section 4.4). This is within-person variety, not diversity across people.

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition: F(1, 208) = 5.05, eta^2 = .024, p = .026. Table 1: Independent M = 6.66, SD = 1.95; AI-Assisted M = 6.06, SD = 2.22. Interaction F(1, 208) = .65, eta^2 = .003, p = .421 (no simple effects reported).

sample_overlap.quote: Although the distribution of participants across conditions was uneven due to the study being nested within a larger project
sample_overlap.locator: p. 4, Section 4 (Method). No other paper using these participants is named; data were collected over two semesters (p. 5).

company_involvement.description: The AI tool is Microsoft Copilot under a university license; no company role in the study is stated. Funding: Marilynn R. Baxter Trust Gift; authors declare no competing interests.

eligibility.reason: The paper states random assignment of individuals to the four cells of a 2 x 2 design whose AI factor is AI-assisted (Copilot) vs independent brainstorming (p. 4). 212 people were analyzed (106 AI-assisted, 106 independent by the cell counts). Outcomes are idea originality, fun, and feasibility rated by blind coders, plus idea count and category count, all scored on the ideas. Caveat: the anticipated-teammate factor was set by arrival (arriving alone meant an AI teammate, p. 5), which contradicts the blanket random-assignment statement for that factor; the paper does not describe how the AI factor was randomized.

one_line_finding: AI-assisted brainstorming produced more original ideas (3.34 vs 2.99; F(1, 208) = 16.78, p < .001) and more fun ideas (3.44 vs 3.18; p = .041) but fewer ideas (11.69 vs 13.24; p = .043) and fewer idea categories (6.06 vs 6.66; p = .026), with the originality and fun gains confined to participants anticipating a human teammate (pp. 6-7, Table 1 p. 9).
open_questions: Was the AI-assistance factor randomized independently of arrival? The paper says all four conditions were randomly assigned, but the teammate factor followed arrival (alone vs paired), so the AI-teammate cells may differ in who arrives alone.
Counts at assignment are not given by cell; 224 were recruited and 12 excluded after assignment (10 for failing condition checks), so the analysis is not intention-to-treat.
ai_available_when_produced is coded yes: in the AI-assisted arms Copilot was available while the scored ideas were produced; the control arms had no AI.
No primary outcome is named; preregistered Hypothesis 1 covers quantity, quality (originality, feasibility, fun), and flexibility together. The OSF preregistration was not checked.
notes: Five output-scored outcomes listed. Impression management (5 self-report items adapted from Wayne and Ferris, 1990; Cronbach's alpha .75) is a manipulation check and is not scored on output, so it is not listed; anticipated human vs AI teammate raised it (F(1, 208) = 93.85, p < .001; p. 6, Section 5.1). Teammate main effects (human vs AI teammate) are not AI-assistance contrasts and are not listed as contrasts: originality F(1, 208) = 7.47, p = .007; fun F(1, 208) = 20.07, p < .001; quantity, feasibility, flexibility not significant (pp. 6-7). Table 1 reports marginal means only (by ideation condition and by teammate), not per-cell means for quantity and flexibility. Analysis: 2 x 2 ANOVA in SPSS 27 with Bonferroni-adjusted simple effects (p. 6, Section 4.5). Coding was done over two semesters with one coder replaced. The md conversion scrambles Table 1; values were checked against PDF p. 9. The candidates.json lead (N = 212, assignment unclear) matches the paper: N = 212 people analyzed.
